But wait: compile with S=16 ms=32: build_costmap ~? 2.8s. But we may have 200 compile requests with FIB total 8192. If each FIB small, costmap building cost ~ per request proportional 128*stride*FIB? Actually build_costmap loops all b 0..127 and e up to stride, and inner over groups total prefixes. For small FIB (say 40), cost is ~128*32*40=163k per request + overhead per (b,e) pair ~ 4096 pairs * groups iteration overhead. 200 requests * maybe 0.02s = 4s. Fine.

But note build_costmap always loops b in 0..127 and for each b builds groups iterating fib; even empty fib 128 iterations. Fine.

Now there's a subtle performance concern: For each (b,e) we iterate over all groups even if many groups have tiny lists; total across groups = number prefixes length>b. Fine.

Compile 2.8s for 2048; aggregate sum FIB 8192 → worst ~ 11s if all in big requests. Fine.

Lookup: aggregate image FIB 8192 total across all lookup requests, addresses total 50000. Our per-address traversal cost depends on path length (S) and branching in edges scanning. For each stage, scanning edges list of current node until match. Edge lists could be large (up to 2048). Worst-case 20000 addresses * S(16) * scan edges... For huge image earlier lookup 7.9s for 20000. But that image FIB was 2048 (from compile). Aggregate across process total image FIB 8192, so up to 4 such 2048 images but then addresses total 50000 → 50000/20000*7.9 ≈ 20s. Fine.

But there is a worst case where edge scanning is O(edges) per stage per address. In big test 7.9s acceptable.
